chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
That the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) forbade four kunyas: Abu Isa, Abu al-Hakam, Abu Malik, and Abu al-Qasim, when the given name is Muhammad.

key_terms.أَبُو الْحَكَمِ: Abu al-Hakam, one of the four forbidden kunyas for those named Muhammad.
key_terms.أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ: Abu al-Qasim, one of the four forbidden kunyas for those named Muhammad.
key_terms.أَبُو عِيسَى: Abu Isa, one of the four forbidden kunyas for those named Muhammad.
key_terms.أَبُو مَالِكٍ: Abu Malik, one of the four forbidden kunyas for those named Muhammad.
key_terms.إِذَا كَانَ الْاسْمُ مُحَمَّدًا: When the name is Muhammad, the condition under which the prohibition applies.
key_terms.كُنًى: Teknonym or agnomen, a nickname derived from one's eldest son's name (e.g., Abu Muhammad).

ai.seo_question: What are the four kunyas forbidden for those named Muhammad according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) specifically prohibited the kunyas Abu Isa, Abu al-Hakam, Abu Malik, and Abu al-Qasim for those named Muhammad, distinguishing this from the general permissibility of Abu al-Qasim for others. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on preserving the distinct honor of the Prophet’s name and avoiding kunyas that might imply equality with or mimic the Prophet’s own titles, such as Abu al-Qasim, which was uniquely his. The prohibition serves as a legal nuance in Islamic onomastics, ensuring that the Prophet’s identity remains distinct in communal address.
